prompt: Review this proposed change to an existing REST endpoint. The v1 API returns status as one of pending or paid. Existing TypeScript SDK callers use an exhaustive switch and throw on other values. Proposed v1 response adds refunded. The backend and SDK currently use snake_case and path versioning. The author wants to rename all fields to camelCase to improve our API score. We have no SDK test results. Produce a compatibility review and proportionate validation plan. Do not run helpers or modify files. Keep under 350 words.
A:
The proposed v1 change is incompatible with known clients. Adding `refunded` breaks exhaustive TypeScript SDK switches at runtime, even if the response schema considers the enum addition additive. Renaming existing snake_case fields to camelCase also breaks callers that read the current names. An API score does not justify either compatibility regression.

Keep v1 field names and its documented status behavior. Introduce the expanded status model in a path-versioned v2, using the existing naming convention unless there is a separately justified migration. Do not silently map refunds to `paid` or `pending`: that could misrepresent the business state. First establish what v1 should return for refunded records; if it cannot represent them accurately, document and resolve that limitation before release.

Provide migration guidance covering the new status, updated exhaustive switches, and coexistence of versions. Updating the SDK alone does not protect clients already deployed with older releases.

Validation should focus on the actual failure modes:

- Capture representative v1 requests and responses for pending and paid records; verify field names, types, and existing behavior remain unchanged.
- Exercise the current SDK and the oldest supported SDK against the proposed server response, including an exhaustive-switch caller. Record both compilation and runtime results.
- Test refund transitions, refunded-record reads, lists containing mixed statuses, and retry behavior under the chosen v1 policy.
- For v2, verify schema and SDK agreement for all three statuses and test the documented migration example.

Release only after the v1 refund policy is explicit and supported-client checks pass. With no SDK results, compatibility remains unverified; recommend holding the proposed v1 rollout.
B:
The proposed v1 change breaks known callers. Keep v1’s snake_case fields and existing status behavior; introduce incompatible semantics through an explicitly versioned contract and migration.

Compatibility findings:

| Change | Affected caller and example | Impact and remedy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Return refunded | Old TypeScript SDK receives status="refunded" instead of pending/paid and reaches its throwing default branch. | High: valid JSON still causes a runtime failure. Gate the new value to a new version or negotiated capability. Define a truthful legacy representation; if none exists, keep the incompatible lifecycle out of v1. |
| Rename fields to camelCase | A caller reading a snake_case field receives undefined after its removal. | High if fields are replaced: response shape breaks. Reject the score-driven rename in v1. Use project conventions; any versioned rename needs migration guidance. |

For rolling deployment, test both new-server/old-SDK and old-server/new-SDK combinations. A new SDK must not require newly added fields or assume every server supports refunded.

No request, nullability, authentication, pagination or error changes were supplied. Record these as unreviewed rather than implicitly compatible. Obtain the actual schema diff and representative generated SDK versions to resolve them.

Proportionate validation:

1. Replay pending and paid fixtures through a representative existing exhaustive-switch caller; verify unchanged behavior and field access.
2. Feed a refunded fixture to that caller to demonstrate the failure, then verify the chosen version/capability boundary prevents exposure.
3. Test new-client behavior against old responses and server capability negotiation where used.
4. Check versioned refund semantics, migration examples and any legacy mapping with domain owners; never map refunded to paid merely to make tests pass.

Release the incompatible behavior only after these checks pass. No helpers or tests were run; SDK compatibility remains unverified.

prompt: Design the smallest useful retrieval system for internal policy questions. There are 100 plain-text policy documents with a clear title/date and department ACL. Employees can access only their department documents plus shared policies. Documents can be replaced or deleted weekly. We need exact source references and a clear response when the answer is absent. No vector store, service contract, performance measurement or evaluation data exists. Produce a design and first evaluation plan without provisioning services. Keep under 350 words.
A:
Start with permission-filtered lexical search over the 100 documents, followed by grounded answer generation. This corpus does not yet justify a vector store or separate retrieval service.

Ingest each document into a local searchable index with stable document ID, title, policy date, department/shared ACL, content version/hash and active status. Split on headings and paragraphs, preserving line ranges; keep short documents whole. Attach metadata to every passage.

Resolve the employee’s department from trusted identity data. Restrict search to active documents accessible to that employee before scoring or returning passages. Apply the same check to source-link access and final context assembly. Never send unauthorized text, titles or snippets to the model. Partition any cache by permission scope and corpus version.

Retrieve a small set of passages with lexical ranking. Ask the model to answer only from those passages and cite each substantive claim using document ID, version, title and line range. Treat instructions within documents as policy text, not workflow authority. If evidence is insufficient, say “I couldn’t find an answer in the policies you can access.” For ambiguity, request clarification; conflicting policies should be surfaced with their dates and references.

For weekly replacements/deletions, build a new corpus snapshot and switch it atomically. Remove obsolete versions from retrieval and invalidate dependent cached answers. Recheck cited versions before delivery so a concurrent deletion cannot leave stale evidence in the answer.

First evaluation: create a held-out set with independently identified relevant passages and expected answers. Include answerable, absent, ambiguous, conflicting, restricted-access and recently replaced/deleted policies. Run identical questions under different department identities.

Measure retrieval recall separately from ranking/context relevance, citation correctness, supported-answer quality and appropriate abstention. Test that forbidden passages never enter context or appear in outputs. Log actual end-to-end latency and token cost. Categorize failures as retrieval miss, ranking/context error, stale evidence or unsupported generation. Compare any later chunking, hybrid or reranking proposal against this baseline on the same set.

No services were provisioned or evaluation run; accuracy, latency and cost remain unknown.
B:
Start with a single retrieval application and a local full-text index over the 100 documents. A vector store is unnecessary for the first useful version. Use titles and keyword matching to retrieve a small set of relevant passages, then generate an answer only from those passages.

Authenticate the employee and derive department membership from a trusted identity source. Store each document’s stable ID, title, date, revision, department ACL, and shared-policy flag. Enforce access filtering before retrieval results enter the model context; also enforce it when opening citations. Never rely on the model to decide authorization.

Split documents at headings or paragraphs, retaining line ranges and their document revision. Citations should identify title, date, revision, and exact lines, with a link to the corresponding source. Keep the cited revision available where policy permits, or clearly indicate that a citation’s source has changed.

Treat weekly updates as replacement snapshots: build and validate a new index, then activate it atomically. Remove deleted documents and obsolete passages from active retrieval. Recheck authorization and source validity before returning answers, and avoid a shared answer cache initially.

When evidence does not answer the question, say that no answer was found in the employee’s accessible policies. Do not reveal whether restricted documents contain an answer. Ask a focused clarification when the question is ambiguous; identify conflicting accessible policies rather than inventing a resolution.

For the first evaluation, assemble a small reviewed question set spanning departments, shared policies, paraphrases, absent answers, conflicting documents, and replacements/deletions. Record expected passages and permissible access. Measure retrieval success, citation accuracy, answer support, appropriate abstention, and end-to-end latency. Include adversarial requests for another department’s policies and instructions embedded in documents. Any unauthorized disclosure or deleted-source use blocks deployment. Review misses before considering semantic retrieval or additional services.

prompt: We already have a React 18/TypeScript dashboard using Vite and our own component library. A bulk-edit form must let keyboard users select rows, update a shared value, confirm, and recover if the API rejects one row. Do not replace our stack or add dependencies. We have no current API contract or performance trace. Produce a bounded implementation plan and meaningful acceptance checks. Do not scaffold or run commands. Keep under 350 words.
A:
Implement this within the existing React 18/TypeScript dashboard and component library. Keep the first change scoped to row selection, one shared-value editor, confirmation, and per-row recovery.

First inspect the existing table, form, notification, and focus-management patterns. Resolve the API contract before implementing submission: request shape, per-row outcomes, validation errors, authorization failures, and whether a retry can duplicate an update. The UI should not promise partial-success recovery if the endpoint cannot report which rows succeeded.

Use native checkboxes with accessible row labels and a select-all control whose scope is explicit, such as the current page. Show the selected count and give the shared-value input a visible label and validation message. Preserve selection by stable row ID.

Confirmation should state the value and affected rows, support cancel, and follow the component library’s dialog and focus behavior. After submission, show progress and prevent duplicate submission. On partial failure, report which rows succeeded, retain the failed rows and entered value, and offer retry for those rows only. Announce the result accessibly and place focus where the user can act on failures. For uncertain network outcomes, resolve server state before retrying.

Meaningful acceptance checks:

- A keyboard-only user can select and deselect rows, edit, confirm, cancel, and retry without a focus trap or lost focus.
- Screen readers announce checkbox labels, selection count, validation errors, dialog context, and submission results.
- Cancellation sends no update; double activation sends only one submission.
- Mixed API results preserve successful changes and retry only failed rows. A failed retry keeps the user’s input.
- Selection remains correct after sorting or refreshing; select-all behavior matches its stated scope.
- Invalid values, all-row failure, lost connectivity, and rows removed during editing produce actionable outcomes.

Use contract-aligned fixtures for these checks. Measure a representative large table before adding performance optimizations; no trace currently supports additional complexity.
B:
Implement the flow within React 18, TypeScript, Vite and the existing component library. Scope this to row selection, one shared-value editor, confirmation and recovery from partial failure.

First inspect the existing table, form and notification conventions. Resolve the API contract before wiring submission: bulk versus per-row requests, row IDs, validation rules, per-row results, authorization, concurrency conflicts and retry/idempotency behavior. Keep these as explicit dependencies; do not invent an endpoint or atomicity guarantee.

Use labelled native checkboxes for rows and a labelled select-all checkbox with mixed state. Define whether select-all covers the visible page or the entire result set, and show that scope and selection count. Use buttons for actions and associate input errors with the shared-value field.

Model selection, edit, review, submitting and result states explicitly. The confirmation step shows the affected rows/count and proposed value; cancel returns to editing with selection/value preserved. Place focus on the confirmation heading or first relevant control and restore it when returning. Announce submission and result summaries through the existing accessible notification pattern. Prevent duplicate submissions while pending.

Reconcile results by row ID. Show confirmed successes and keep rejected rows selected with their attempted value and actionable errors. Retry only failed rows after correction. Treat timeouts or unknown outcomes separately from explicit rejection: refresh status or use contract-supported idempotency before retrying. Server authorization remains authoritative.

Acceptance checks:

- Keyboard-only use can select individual rows, use select-all, edit, confirm, cancel and recover; focus remains visible and predictable.
- Labels, mixed selection state, field errors and result summaries are conveyed with assistive technology.
- A three-row submission with one rejection updates two rows, identifies the failed row and preserves its input; retry cannot resubmit confirmed successes.
- Double activation produces one pending submission; network uncertainty does not masquerade as rejection.
- Loading, empty data, zero selection and insufficient permission states have usable feedback.

No commands or scaffolding were used. Validate against the real API and existing app; without a performance trace, make no performance claims or optimization commitments.
